text: DP-750 doesn't ask 'what is a catalog binding' — it describes a situation and asks what you'd actually do. This lesson drills that reasoning skill, one situation from each of this course's six chapters.

A finance team needs aggregates visible but customer names hidden on individual transactions. The answer is a column mask scoped to a group — one table, different views by role, not a second duplicated catalog.

A pipeline ingesting millions of files a day times out doing directory listing on every run. File notification mode exists exactly for this — subscribing to storage events instead of listing the tree each time.

A silver table needs to drop negative order totals without failing the whole run. That's an expect-or-drop expectation, not fail-update, which would halt the pipeline instead of just filtering the bad rows.
A job has one task feeding two independent tasks that both feed a final task. That's a dependency graph — the middle tasks run in parallel, and the final task depends on both finishing.
A big join runs fine on most partitions but crawls on a handful. That's data skew, and Adaptive Query Execution can detect and split those partitions automatically.
A pipeline needs a database password without hard-coding it in a notebook anyone can open. That's secrets management — stored in a secret scope, resolved only at runtime.
Six scenarios, six chapters, one pattern: a constraint that rules out the obvious wrong answer, and one feature that fits precisely. Next up: the capstone that ties all of it together.
